Tiny machines / A first fabrication lesson

How to build a tiny diving board

Build a beam on temporary support. Remove the support. Keep the anchor. That is the central trick behind many suspended MEMS structures.

MEMS means microelectromechanical systems: tiny structures that can move, sense, or act. This lesson explains one simplified surface-micromachining approach; other processes use different recipes.

Teal: structure that staysAmber: temporary supportPurple: patterning stencil

The icons are visual analogies, not cross-sections or fabrication drawings. Real MEMS anchors are not bolted diving-board posts.

The six-step build

Start with a foundation

A silicon wafer is the base. Insulating and electrical layers may be added before the mechanical structure.

Lay down temporary support

Deposit a sacrificial layer, often an oxide. Gas-based chemistry can grow a solid coating across the surface. Its thickness helps set the future clearance.

Open a place to attach

Pattern and etch an opening through the support where the beam must attach. This is where the structural material will connect to the foundation.

Deposit and shape the beam

Add structural material over the support and into the anchor opening. Pattern and etch that material to define the beam’s outline. The temporary support is still underneath.

Remove the temporary support

A selective release etch removes the sacrificial material while leaving the structure sufficiently intact. Wide plates may need holes so the etchant can reach underneath.

Let the beam move

The anchor stays connected while the rest of the beam is suspended. Release and drying must avoid making the beam stick to the surface.

How do they “draw” the shapes?

Coat the surface with photoresist, a light-sensitive material. Expose a pattern, develop openings, etch the exposed material below, then strip the resist. The protected areas survive that etch.

Photoresist is a temporary stencil. A sacrificial layer is a temporary support. They are not the same thing. Depending on the resist, exposed or unexposed regions can be removed during development.

Do they scrape each layer flat?

Your intuition is close for processes with planarization. Chemical-mechanical polishing uses a pad and slurry to remove high spots and flatten a surface.

But many deposited coatings follow existing bumps. Polishing is a specified process step, not something the foundry automatically does after every layer. That matters when one structure crosses another.

Your design playground has boundaries

On a standard shared run, you usually draw flat patterns within a fixed fabrication recipe. Those patterns collectively produce a three-dimensional device.

The foundry usually fixesYou usually choose
Materials and layer orderOutlines on each permitted layer
Layer thicknesses and vertical clearancesBeam lengths, widths and arrangements
Etching and polishing stepsLocations of anchors and release openings
Minimum sizes, gaps and overlapsGeometry that obeys those rules

Think in patterned layers, not arbitrary 3D sculptures. A custom process can change the boundaries, but requires additional development.

Three traps worth knowing

“A huge plate should release just like a thin beam.”

The etchant needs a route underneath. A broad plate may need release holes; the process handbook specifies acceptable geometry and spacing.

“Once released, the beam must be perfectly flat.”

Residual stress and stress gradients can deform structures. Geometry, materials and processing affect the final shape. Simulation and fabrication measurements help you check it.

“If the drawing passes the rules, the device must work.”

Rule checks help with manufacturability. You still need to check mechanics, electrical readout, unwanted contact, release, packaging and the task you want it to perform.

Try the two-question check

Why doesn’t the beam fall off when the support disappears?

The structural material connects to the foundation at the anchor. The release removes the temporary support, not that intended connection.

Can you make one beam twice as thick just by drawing it wider?

No. Width is an in-plane choice; thickness comes from the deposited layer. A wider beam can behave differently, but does not become twice as thick.

Your first useful design exercise

Choose one foundry process. Find its layer-stack diagram. Draw a beam and an anchor, identify the sacrificial material beneath it, and trace how the release etchant reaches that material. Only then start changing the geometry.

For your future AI-driven chip, start by understanding one repeatable physical response before combining many structures.
